title: the summit sit
hook: the Mahabharata nears its end on a mountain road, with a dog walking behind a king

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the practices with Sanskrit sounds for readers, the alphabet heard before it is seen. Did one of those sounds stay in your mouth? Today the last block of the year begins. Day one thousand forty-seven.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `THE ALPHABET, IN SOUND.`

segments.voice: Near the end of the Mahabharata, the five Pandava brothers and Draupadi leave their kingdom on foot. A dog falls in behind them and keeps walking. At last they turn north, toward the mountains. On the slope, one walker falls, then another, then another. Yudhishthira, the eldest, keeps going and does not look back. Only the dog is still beside him when a chariot comes down to meet him. This week opens the year's last block, and its days share one name: the summit sit. Each day climbs back to one stretch of the year and sits there. Today, the great story.
screen: `FIVE BROTHERS, DRAUPADI, AND A DOG.` → `ONE BY ONE, THEY FALL.` → `A WEEK OF SUMMIT SITS.`

segments.voice: The walk has a book of its own inside the epic, the Book of the Great Journey. As each walker falls, Bhima asks his brother why, and Yudhishthira names a cause: a pride, a partiality, an appetite, something each one carried the whole way up. He does not stop to mourn. He walks on. Then Indra, king of the gods, arrives in his chariot and invites Yudhishthira to rise to heaven in his own body. There is one condition. The dog stays behind. Yudhishthira refuses. In the story's words, paraphrased: to abandon one who is devoted to you, one who is frightened and has no other refuge, is a grave wrong, and he will not do it, not even for heaven. Indra argues. Yudhishthira holds. And then the dog changes form. It was Dharma himself, the god of righteousness, who in the story is Yudhishthira's own father, testing his son again, as he once did as the Yaksha at the lake. Now step back and see the whole story from up here. The snake sacrifice that frames it. Bhishma's vow. The dice game and Draupadi's question. The Yaksha at the lake. The battlefield and the Gita spoken on it. Gandhari's grief. A story that size could have closed on a war. Near its end it stops instead on a tired man who will not leave a dog on a mountain. Whatever else dharma means across all those books, this test of it is small, and personal, and costs a great deal.
screen: `THE BOOK OF THE GREAT JOURNEY.` · `ONE BY ONE, THE WALKERS FALL.` · `NOT WITHOUT THE DOG.` · `THE DOG WAS DHARMA.` · then, large: `A SMALL LOYALTY, AT THE TOP.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably for the bell's two minutes. Let the great story walk past you, one figure at a time: Bhishma, Kunti, Karna, Draupadi, Arjuna, Gandhari, Yudhishthira. Don't hold on to any of them. Let each one go by. If one stays, notice who it is, and let that be all right. In the last breaths, bring to mind someone who has walked beside you through a hard stretch of your own road. Just their face. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. A week of sitting at the top of the year and looking back at one stretch at a time. Today's stretch: the great story, and the dog at its end.

Your line: the summit sit. Today, notice one being that stays beside you without being asked: a friend, a coworker, an animal. Stay beside it a little longer than you need to. Day one thousand forty-seven.

howItsDone: The Mahabharata lives in recitations, retellings, plays and television serials; the story of Yudhishthira refusing heaven without the dog is retold as a teaching about loyalty and dharma.

fork.setup: you are Yudhishthira. Indra's chariot is waiting to take you to heaven, but he says the dog cannot come. what do you do?
options: leave the dog and climb into the chariot.
refuse heaven rather than abandon the dog.
ask Indra for a day to think it over.
fork.reveal: he refuses: abandoning one who is devoted and has no other refuge is a wrong he won't commit, even for heaven. Then the dog reveals itself as Dharma.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: dharma, right order and right conduct; also the name of the god who takes the dog's form.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Mahabharata is a war story that ends with the war.
what it means: near its end, the epic tests its hero with a dog on a mountain road, long after the battle.
what a scholar hears: the Mahaprasthanika Parva, the Book of the Great Journey, where Dharma tests Yudhishthira before the epic's final book.

notes: First of seven summit sits (1047–1053), opening the block 'Festivals held; year close'. Each summit sit revisits one stretch of year three; this one revisits the Mahabharata serial (697–879). The outline gives no word, practice or hook for these days, so the plan (one block of the year per day) is the writer's; confirm.

Paraphrase of Mahaprasthanika Parva: Yudhishthira's refusal to abandon a devoted, frightened creature with no other refuge; Indra's condition; the dog revealed as Dharma. The causes Yudhishthira names for each fall are summarized, not listed; check the summary 'a pride, a partiality, an appetite'.
The epic continues after this book (Svargarohana Parva), so the script says 'near its end', not 'at its end'. Confirm 'rise to heaven in his own body' as a fair paraphrase of Indra's offer.
Ganguli's translation (1883–1896) is public domain but not on the validator's list, so nothing is quoted.
Editor pass: 'serial' changed to 'story' in the teach; dropped the day count from the hook (curriculum count, not a text claim).

Audit 2026-10-01: 'testing him one last time' and 'a last test' were wrong: in the Svargarohana Parva Dharma tests Yudhishthira again (the illusion of hell), and Dharma had tested him before as the Yaksha. Now 'testing his son again, as he once did as the Yaksha at the lake'. The route is east, south, west, then north, so 'at last they turn north'.
